zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after the independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510; supplied page subset, CC BY 4.0. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ This aid supports lexical identification, not this copy's glyphs, spacing, or typeface.

lines.note: Naburi means mocking or making fun of someone, matching both Portuguese verbs. The initial is a damaged capital N, not OCR x; the printed abbreviated principal parts u, utta are retained.

runs.text: Peßoa de que ſe zomba, ou mo

lines.note: Naburimono is a person made an object of ridicule. The final mo belongs to moteja on the following row; no terminal hyphen is visible here.
Teja completes moteja. Naburimono ni naru means becoming an object of mockery; the translation starts the passive ser zombado, with the printed nasal abbreviation in zõ-.
Completes the preceding passive translation: being mocked and scorned. This short continuation belongs to Naburimono rather than to the next entry.
Naca covers inside, middle, and between, then introduces the relational sense of friendship. Amiza continues as amizade below; the unhyphenated physical division is preserved.
Naca wo chigau is breaking off friendly relations. The visible gloss reads Quebrar, not OCR Qusbrar; the Japanese final caron in chigǒ is retained without modernizing the contracted form.
Naca wo naosu means repairing relations or making peace. The Portuguese contrasts this reconciliation with the rupture described immediately above.

runs.text: Meo da couſa que ſe vai fazendo, &

lines.note: Nacaba denotes the middle of an activity in progress, rather than only a spatial centre. The coordinated Portuguese description continues onto the following row.

runs.text: continuando como meo da meſa, lição, &c.

lines.note: The examples illustrate being midway through a meal or a lesson. Historical meo and the printed meſa are kept rather than replaced by modern vocabulary.

runs.text: Eſpinha grande, que està no meo

lines.note: Nacabone is the large central fishbone or backbone. The relative clause locates it in the middle, with its object supplied on the short next row.
Do peixe completes the description of the central bone of a fish. It is a complete physical continuation line, not an independent gloss.
Nacadacana describes something raised in the middle. The repeated Naca- begins the compound example continued below, and its printed hyphen is visible.
Completes nacadacana cauo, a face with a raised central profile. The Portuguese introduces a particular use among women, explained more fully in the next two rows.

runs.text: por roſto que tem o nariz aleuantado, & mais

lines.note: The phrase is interpreted as a face with a high, projecting nose. The final mais modifies the following description, not a second headword.
Saido pera fora completes the image of a nose projecting outward. The historical phrase and its unaccented spelling are preserved.
Nacadachi is an intermediary, including a marriage broker and, in the divided final word, a procurer. Caſamenteiro is one printed word, not OCR Ca ſamenteiro.
Couiteiro completes Alcouiteiro. Nacadachi wo suru means acting as such an intermediary; the Portuguese verb Fazer is divided after Fa-.
Completes Fazer estes officios, performing the intermediary roles just enumerated. Officios refers to those functions rather than to a separate occupation entry.

runs.text: Sebe que ſe faz no meo pera di-

lines.note: Nacagaqi is a dividing hedge or fence erected in the middle. The Portuguese purpose clause begins the divided noun divisão.
The hedge separates something into parts; nacagaqi wo suru illustrates making that partition. The tilde is over u in dalgũa, and Vt is printed in the italic apparatus.
The translation means making this hedge, directly explaining the preceding Japanese example. The provisional st classification in esta is retained rather than globally regularized.

runs.text: Meo tempo, tendo reſpeito ao prin-

lines.note: Nacagoro denotes a middle period relative to a beginning and an end. The physical line divides principio after prin-.

runs.text: cipio, ou fim quer ſeja de hum anno, ou mes.

lines.note: Completes the contrast between beginning and end, whether of a year or a month. The scan supports fim, not OCR ſim; the Portuguese temporal comparison confirms the word identity.

runs.text: Couſas que ſe dizem de hum pera

lines.note: Nacagoto concerns remarks about someone intended to damage relations. The purpose clause is unfinished here and continues with causing a break with another person.
The remarks are intended to make one person fall out with another. The repeated headword begins an example and remains divided from its object particle by the physical line break.
Nacagoto wo yuu means saying things that cause discord. The translation supplies the hostile interpersonal sense rather than neutral conversation between people.
Nacaguro describes arrows blackened at the middle; the example is nacaguro no soya. Fre- begins the Portuguese plural for arrows on the next row.

runs.text: chas vruxadas de preto no meo.

lines.note: Completes Frechas: arrows lacquered black in the middle. Vruxadas is retained as the dictionary's Portuguese description of lacquer treatment.

runs.text: Molheres de ſeruiço que não ſão das

lines.note: Naca-i denotes women in service who are not of the lowest rank. Enlargement shows an internal hyphen before i, omitted in the OCR; it is not a physical line-end division.
Completes the qualification that these servants are not the lowest-ranking women in service. The short row belongs to Naca-i.

runs.text: Dia do meo que fica entre dous.

lines.note: Nacaichijit denotes a full intervening day between two other days. The final t is the historical checked ending and is not expanded to a modern Japanese syllable.

The example describes staying for one intervening day. The scan visibly separates Naca ichijit here, unlike the headword above. Tôriǔ refers to a stay or sojourn; itaita is retained as the historical past form rather than modernized.

runs.text: hum dia inteiro, & parte do em que cheguei, &

lines.note: The stay includes one whole day and part of the arrival day. The next row adds part of the departure day, clarifying exactly what the intervening day excludes.

runs.text: parte do em que me parti.

lines.note: Completes the stay with part of the day of departure. The three physical rows together explain one complete day between arrival and departure.
Naca ichinen similarly means an intervening year between two others. The visible space after Naca is preserved, unlike the joined preceding day expression.

runs.text: Lugar do meo dalbarda do caualo que

lines.note: Nacaje names the central place in a horse's pack saddle. The scan supports Lugar rather than OCR Lagar; the relative clause continues with its position between the side loads.
Specifies the space between the two side loads or panniers. The final upright B. is the dictionary's low-register label, not part of the italic Portuguese sentence.

runs.text: Ilha que eſtà no meo do rio, ou do

lines.note: Nacajima is an island in the middle of a river or sea. The surviving i and m support jima, correcting OCR juna and the resulting misleading kana hint.

runs.text: mar. ¶ Item, Ilha que fazem artificioſa-

lines.note: Completes the sea-island sense and adds an artificial island. Artificioſa- continues with mente on the next row, retaining the visible terminal hyphen.
The artificial island is made in the middle of a pond. This explains the second sense of Nacajima without assigning a particular garden tradition not named in the gloss.
Nacamichi means the middle road or path. The damaged medial type is m, supported by its surviving strokes and Caminho, not OCR n in Nacanichi.
Nacanaca is here an affirmative adverb, yes or indeed. This explicitly recorded historical sense should not be replaced by the better-known modern negative-polarity construction.

runs.text: Adu. Aſsi como aßi milhor he,

lines.note: Nacanacani introduces the sense that something would be better anyway or rather. The scan separates Aſsi como and has aßi without the OCR's extra s.
The example means that dying would be preferable. The Japanese xinda ga maxi gia is printed with the observed joined forms, not respaced into modern analytical units.

runs.text: Aßi como aßi milhor he morrer.

lines.note: The Portuguese explicitly translates the preceding example as it being better to die anyway. This flush-left continuation remains body text, not a new headword.
Nacanacano coto supplies an emphatic affirmative response, rendered by Pois não? and yes. The initial is N, correcting OCR V and its erroneous derived reading.
Nacanauori denotes making peace or restoring friendship. The example begins with Na- and continues on the final physical row of this column.
Completes nacanauori wo suru, to reconcile or make peace. The scan places this continuation at the ordinary continuation indent; the stable ID is retained while its placement is corrected.

runs.text: Fato que vai no caualo entre os dous

lines.note: Nacani is the load carried on a horse between the two side loads. The final s of dous is visible against the right rule and is restored from the incomplete OCR dou.
Coſtais completes the two side loads or panniers flanking the central burden. This refers to their placement, complementing Nacaje in the preceding column.
Nacanimo means especially or particularly. The dictionary labels it an adverb and provides the direct Portuguese equivalent.
Nacanzzucu is another expression for especially, corresponding to nakanzuku. The double z is part of the printed historical spelling and is not simplified.
Nacara denotes half a measure of anything. The vowel sequence in qualquer corrects OCR quelquer without altering the historical feminine mea.
Nacarabi first describes a tide halfway out. Enlargement shows a small grave over the final e of Marè; the repeated Japanese form is divided after Nacara-.

Completes nacarabi de gozaru, saying that the tide is half out. The small mark over marẽ is worn; the aligned OCR's tilde is provisionally retained, rather than copied from the preceding grave-marked occurrence.

runs.text: Couſa que eſta mea enxuta, ou ſeca. Vt,

lines.note: Adds the sense of something half dried. The example starts with Na- and continues on the next row; the two senses share incomplete drying or withdrawal of water.

Completes nacarabini fita, illustrating the half-dry state. The printed fita is retained as the form associated with drying, not replaced by an anticipated xita; the Portuguese directly confirms the state described.
Ou seca completes the alternative Portuguese wording for being half dry. It belongs to the preceding example rather than introducing a separate sense.
Nacatagai denotes a falling-out or rupture of friendship. Its gloss connects directly with the earlier Naca example about breaking relations.

runs.text: Eſteira de dous juncos de largo,

lines.note: This Nacatçugui names a mat made from two lengths of rushes across its width. The following row explains how the rushes are joined at the middle.

runs.text: juntos, & tecidos no meo do aueſo. Vt,

lines.note: The rushes are joined and woven at the centre on the reverse side. The single printed long s in aueſo is preserved rather than doubled from modern avesso.
Nacatçugui no omote repeats the name for this mat surface. The initial vowel is a, not OCR u; the printed vomote spelling is preserved.
A separate homonymous entry describes a particular round lacquered container. It must not be merged with the preceding mat entry merely because the headword is identical.

runs.text: que ſerue de ter Cha moido.

lines.note: The container holds powdered tea. The scan reads ſerue, not OCR ſerae; Cha is a Japanese term embedded in the Portuguese explanation and is recorded for optional whole-word typeface review.

runs.text: Segũda nouidade do arroz, ou arroz

lines.note: Nacate denotes rice maturing after the earliest crop, here described as the second harvest or crop. The nasal abbreviation in Segũda remains unexpanded.

runs.text: que vem mais tarde, logo depois do primej-

lines.note: Specifies rice arriving later, immediately after the first. The printed primej- is retained at the division before ro, including its descending final letter rather than modernizing primeiro.

runs.text: ro. O mais temporão ſe diz, Vaxe. O mais

lines.note: Completes the preceding word and names the earliest-ripening rice Vaxe, corresponding to wase. Vaxe is embedded within Portuguese naming syntax, so it is included in the typeface-term mapping.
Names the late-ripening rice Vocute, corresponding to okute. The Portuguese ſorodeo contrasts with temporão above; Vocute is another embedded Japanese term rather than a new headword here.
Nacauobi introduces examples of being dressed with a sash but without outer garments. The upright l supplies an alternative expression, whose nacauo- continues below.
Completes nacauobi bacaride, being only girt with a sash. Enlargement shows no tilde over the o of ſomente; the OCR's nasal mark is removed.
Specifies the absence of trousers and a Dobuco outer garment. The word Dobuco is embedded Japanese within the Portuguese clause; the broken ascender of b is not supplied as an accent on o.
Nacauori is identified simply as a kind of paper with this name. The gloss does not justify supplying a particular manufacturing method or modern paper category.

runs.text: Certa laya de frechas mais esti-

lines.note: Nacazaxi names a particular, more highly valued kind of arrow. The Portuguese adjective is divided after esti-; its provisional st classification is retained.
Completes estimadas, valued or esteemed, qualifying the arrows above. The short continuation is real body text despite the nearby ink blemish at its beginning.
Nacazora denotes the region of the air or mid-sky. The explanation is spatial and supplies no additional cosmological classification.

runs.text: Nuuens do ceo, ou do ar.

lines.note: Nacazora no cumo means clouds in the sky or air. The Portuguese historical spellings Nuuens and ceo are preserved.

runs.text: Riſca que ſe deita pello meo do

lines.note: Nacazumi is an inked centre line. The description begins with drawing a line through the middle and identifies the wooden surface on the following row.
The line is drawn with ink along a piece of wood or board. This completes the carpenter's marking sense rather than referring simply to black coloration.
Naccu is labelled an adverb with several meanings and uses. The ensuing examples concern unexpectedly early or easy completion and arrival; the double c is retained.
Naccu xifataita means finishing sooner or more easily than expected, as the continuation explains. The scan has Naccu, not OCR Xaccu; xifataita retains the historical s-stem past formation.

runs.text: quando menos cuidaua, ou mais cedo, & com

lines.note: The speaker finished when least expecting it, or sooner, and with greater ease. The unfinished comparison continues onto the next physical row.

runs.text: mais facilidade do que ſe eſperaua. ¶

lines.note: Completes the comparison with what had been expected. The next illustration begins with the divided Nac-, which is not a separate lexical form.
Completes Naccu tçuita, arriving sooner than expected. The example's arrival verb contrasts with the preceding completion verb while illustrating the same adverb.
Cuidaua completes the comparison with the speaker's expectation. The Portuguese verb here concerns thinking or expecting, not taking care of someone.
Nacǒdo is a go-between or intermediary, not the ordinal third in this context. The open-long-o caron is visible and is not replaced by the modern nakoudo spelling.

runs.text: Borda do mar, ou junto da terra.

lines.note: Nada is glossed as the sea edge or water close to land. The example begins with Na-, retained at the physical division rather than generalized to every modern use of nada.
Nada wo noru is sailing along the coast. The visible word is longo, correcting OCR lengo; the gloss specifically keeps the vessel near land.
Nadamari denotes becoming pacified or subsiding. The reflexive Portuguese verbs distinguish this intransitive entry from the transitive Nadame that follows.
Icari ga nadamaru means anger subsiding. Enlargement supports Abrandarſe, correcting the OCR's Abrandas ſe; the Portuguese infinitive describes the calming of the anger itself.
Nadame means soothing or mitigating something. The printed principal-part abbreviation uru is preserved rather than rewritten to the modern verb form.
Fito no cocoro wo nadamuru means soothing another person's heart or feelings. The object-marked construction supplies the transitive counterpart to anger subsiding above.
Completes Aplacar and adds comforting someone. The Portuguese translation confirms that the preceding Japanese example is emotional reassurance, not flattening a physical surface.
Nadaracana first describes something even and level, then announces a metaphorical extension. The medial r is visible; OCR Nadatacana is corrected without altering the printed Permet. abbreviation.
Nadaracana fito applies the adjective to a gentle person. The following short row completes the pair of Portuguese character descriptions.
Manſo completes the metaphorical sense as mild or meek. The signature and Nad below are page furniture, not continuations of this gloss.
This anticipates Nadaracani at the beginning of the next supplied page; it is not an additional body entry.
